why: Tracing a dial's turns to a hidden stack of wheels helps your child explain a step-by-step cause with pictures and words.
teaser: Spin a padlock dial and follow a hidden train of wheels, pegs and notches until a thin fence drops in.
title: How Combo Locks Work
question: How can a turning dial remember three secret numbers?
idea: A combination lock hides a stack of loose wheels, each with one notch called a gate. Pegs let the dial pick the wheels up one by one, and each turn back leaves a set wheel behind. When all the gates line up, a thin bar called a fence drops in and the lock opens.

curiosity.intro: Start with a padlock on the kitchen table. Then peek at the wheels inside, pick them up one by one, watch the fence drop and visit an old safe.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you see a dial lock, count its turns and picture the wheels lining up.

questions.question: What is hiding behind the dial?
questions.notice: Follow the row from the dial to the drive cam, three wheels and a thin bar.
questions.say: Behind the dial sits a drive cam, a disc fixed to the dial with one short peg. Next come three flat wheels on one rod. Each wheel has a notch called a gate. The thin bar is the fence. The wheels are loose, so they turn only when something pushes them.
questions.try: Cut three paper circles and snip a small notch in each. Stack them on a pencil. Can you turn them so all three notches line up?

questions.question: Why do you spin the dial three times first?
questions.notice: Find the tab on each wheel and the spot where one tab touches the next.
questions.say: The cam's peg travels almost a full turn before it bumps the first wheel. That wheel then needs nearly a turn to catch the second, and the second to catch the third. Three spins make sure every wheel is moving. Then the wheel farthest from the dial is set first.
questions.try: Tie three toy cars together with loose string. Pull the front one slowly. Watch each car start to move only when its string goes tight.

questions.question: What has to happen for the lock to open?
questions.notice: Compare the stack with gates in a line to the stack with gates pointing every way.
questions.say: The fence rests on the smooth edges of the wheels. It can drop only when all three gates sit in one straight line beneath it. If even one gate points the wrong way, the fence stays up and the lock stays shut.
questions.try: Set out three cups with their handles pointing different ways. Turn them until every handle points the same way, like gates in a row.

questions.question: Can a number that is close still open a lock?
questions.notice: Find the big dial on the safe door and the fine marks around its edge.
questions.say: Each gate is a little wider than the fence, so being one mark off can still work. Testers check that good safe locks open only within about one mark of each number. Some very strong locks use plastic wheels that are hard to see in X-ray pictures. They also keep the fence lifted off the wheels, so nobody can feel it.
questions.try: Hide a toy under one of ten cups in a row. Let a helper guess. Does it help if you say “close” when they are one cup away?

beats.title: Three secret numbers

beats.title: Wheels in a stack
beats.passage: Behind the dial hides a stack of three flat wheels on one thin rod. Each wheel has one small notch in its edge, called a gate. The wheels sit loose, so they do not turn when the dial starts to move. In front of them is a drive cam, a disc fixed to the dial. It has one short peg.
beats.prompt: What is the small notch on each wheel called?

foldable.heading: Wheels in a stack

beats.title: Picking up the wheels
beats.passage: Turn the dial, and the cam's peg swings round. After almost a full turn, it bumps a tab on the nearest wheel and drags it along. That wheel's own peg catches the next wheel, and that one catches the last. So you spin three times first, like an engine hooking three train cars.
beats.prompt: Why do you spin the dial three times first?

foldable.heading: Picking up the wheels
foldable.body: Each wheel's peg catches the next one. Three spins pick up all three wheels, like an engine hooking train cars.

beats.title: Back and forth
beats.passage: Here is a clue. Stop on the first number, and the farthest wheel is set. Now turn the other way. The pegs let go, so that wheel stays put. You pass the first number once, because the cam needs a full turn to pick up the middle wheel. Stop on the second number. Then turn back to the third.
beats.prompt: Why do you pass the first number once?

foldable.heading: Back and forth
foldable.body: Each turn the other way leaves a set wheel behind. Pass the first number once to pick up the middle wheel.

beats.title: The fence drops in
beats.passage: Back at the table, Big Wonderer pulls on the lock. Pop! The shackle swings open, and the little one points. Now the guess changes. The lock never remembered any numbers. The wheels just stayed where they were left. When all three gates line up, a thin bar called a fence drops in and frees the shackle.
beats.prompt: What drops into the lined-up gates?

foldable.heading: The fence drops in
foldable.body: The lock keeps no numbers. When all three gates line up, a thin bar called a fence drops in.

beats.title: Close enough
beats.passage: Here is a surprise. Each gate is a little wider than the fence, so a number one off can often still open a lock! Safe makers test locks so they open only very close to each number. Experts can feel tiny bumps as the fence brushes the wheels. So the best safe locks hold the fence away. How could a lock give away no clues?
beats.prompt: Why can a number that is one off still work?

foldable.body: Gates are a bit wider than the fence, so one number off can still work. How could a lock hide its clues?

beats.passage: Behind the dial hides a stack of three flat wheels threaded on one thin rod. Each wheel has a single small notch in its edge, called a gate. The wheels sit loose, so they do not turn when the dial first starts to move. In front of them is the drive cam. It is a disc fixed to the dial, with one short peg sticking out.

beats.passage: When you turn the dial, the cam's peg swings round with it. After almost one full turn, the peg bumps a small tab on the nearest wheel and drags that wheel along. The wheel has its own peg, which catches the second wheel, and that one catches the third. This is why you spin the dial three times first. It picks up all three wheels, like an engine hooking train cars.

beats.passage: Here is a clue that makes the idea easier to trust. Stop on the first number, and the wheel farthest from the dial is set. Now turn the other way. The pegs let go, so that far wheel stays exactly where it is. You pass the first number once, because the cam needs a full turn to pick up the middle wheel. beats.passage: Back at the table, Big Wonderer pulled on the lock, and pop, the shackle swung open while the little one pointed. Now the guess changed. The lock had never remembered any numbers at all; the wheels simply stayed where they were left. A thin bar called a fence rests on their edges. When all three gates line up beneath it, the fence drops in and frees the shackle.
beats.prompt: Where does the lock keep the combination?

beats.passage: Here is a surprise. Each gate is a little wider than the fence, so a number that is one off can often still open the lock. How would you build a lock that gives away no clues?

beats.passage: Little Wonderer found a padlock lying on the kitchen table, its round black dial marked with forty numbers running from 0 to 39. beats.passage: Behind the dial hides a stack of three flat wheels threaded on one thin rod, a set that lock makers call the wheel pack. Each wheel has a single small notch in its edge, called a gate. The wheels sit loose on the rod, so they do not turn when the dial first starts to move. In front of them is the drive cam, a disc fixed to the dial with one short peg sticking out of its face.
beats.prompt: What do lock makers call the stack of wheels?

beats.passage: When you turn the dial, the cam's peg swings round with it. After almost one full turn, the peg bumps a small tab on the nearest wheel, called a fly, and drags that wheel along. That wheel has its own peg on its far side, which catches the second wheel's fly, and the second wheel catches the third. This is why you spin three times first, picking up all three wheels like an engine hooking train cars. Strangely, the wheel farthest from the dial is the one that sets the first number.
beats.prompt: Which wheel sets the first number?

beats.passage: Here is a clue that makes the idea easier to trust. Stop on the first number, and the wheel farthest from the dial is set. Now turn the other way: the pegs let go, so that far wheel stays exactly where it is. You pass the first number once, because the cam needs a full turn to catch the middle wheel again. Then you stop on the second number and turn back to the third, which moves only the nearest wheel. Many large safes use four wheels and even more turns.
beats.prompt: Why would a four-wheel safe need more turns?

beats.passage: Back at the table, Big Wonderer pulled on the lock, and with a pop the shackle swung open while the little one pointed. Now the guess changed. The lock had never remembered any numbers at all; the wheels simply stayed wherever they were left, like bookmarks. A thin bar called a fence rests on their smooth edges. When all three gates line up beneath it, the fence drops into the slot they make, and the shackle is free to pull out.
beats.prompt: How are the wheels like bookmarks?

beats.passage: Here is a surprise: each gate is a little wider than the fence, so a number that is one off can often still open the lock. Safe makers test their best locks so they open only within about one mark of each number. Experts can feel tiny bumps as the fence brushes the wheels. So strong safe locks hold the fence up and away, and some use plastic wheels that hide in X-ray pictures. How would you build a lock that gives away no clues?
beats.prompt: What two tricks help a safe lock hide its clues?

poem.title: The Secret on the Lock
lines: Little Wonderer spun the black dial of a lock,
three turns to the right, tick, tick, tickety-tock.
“There are wheels in there, hiding, all stacked in a row,
and each has a notch where a fence wants to go.”
“Turn left, pass the first,” the big one said, “then
stop on the second, and back right again.
When all of the gates line up, one, two, three,
the fence will drop in, and the shackle swings free.”
“But what if I lose them?” the little one cried.
“Three numbers are slippery. They wriggle and hide!”
So out came a pencil, and out came some tape,
and a note went right onto the lock’s steely shape.
“Now I’ll never forget them! They’re right there in sight!”
Big Wonderer peeked through two mittens. “That’s right…
your secret is safe, for it never can go,
except that now everyone else gets to know.”
